species.summary: Florida's last wild big cat and one of the most endangered mammals in the country.
species.description: The Florida panther is a subspecies of puma that once ranged across the Southeast. Today the only known breeding population lives in southern Florida, in and around Big Cypress National Preserve and the Everglades.
species.habitat: Hardwood hammocks, pine flatwoods, cypress swamps, and prairies.
threats: Habitat loss and fragmentation from development
Vehicle collisions on roads that cross panther territory
Territorial fights between males in a small, crowded range
Low genetic diversity in a small population
identification_tips: Adults are a uniform tawny tan with a paler belly and no spots
Long tail with a dark tip
Kittens have dark spots and ringed tails that fade as they grow
how_to_help: Slow down in wildlife speed zones on roads through panther habitat
Never feed wildlife, so animals don't lose their wariness of people
Support protection of large, connected natural areas
Report injured or dead panthers to Florida Fish and Wildlife (FWC)

species.summary: A gentle, slow-moving sea cow that grazes on seagrass in warm shallow water.
species.description: Florida manatees are large, plant-eating marine mammals that use coastal waters, rivers, and canals. In cold weather they gather at warm springs and other warm-water refuges.
species.habitat: Warm, shallow coastal waters, estuaries, rivers, and canals with seagrass or other aquatic plants.
threats: Collisions with boats
Loss of seagrass from poor water quality
Cold stress in winter
Harmful algal blooms such as red tide
identification_tips: Gray-brown, rounded body about 9 to 10 feet long
Flat, paddle-shaped tail
Whiskered, blunt snout; surfaces to breathe
how_to_help: Follow manatee zones and slow-speed signs when boating
Wear polarized sunglasses to spot manatees below the surface
Observe from a distance and never feed or give water to manatees
Pick up fishing line and trash; report injured or dead manatees to FWC

species.summary: A tall wading bird that feeds by feel in shrinking dry-season pools.
species.description: The wood stork is Florida's only native stork. It nests in colonies and depends on wetlands that concentrate fish as water levels fall in the dry season.
species.habitat: Freshwater and brackish wetlands, cypress swamps, and mangroves.
threats: Loss of wetland feeding areas
Changes in water flow that disrupt the timing of prey concentration
Disturbance of nesting colonies
identification_tips: Large white wading bird with black flight feathers
Bald, dark gray head and neck
Long, thick bill that curves slightly downward
how_to_help: Keep your distance from nesting colonies and feeding flocks
Support restoration of natural water flow in the Everglades
Protect wetlands on and near your property

species.summary: A slender hawk with a hooked bill built for eating apple snails.
species.description: The Everglade snail kite hunts almost entirely for apple snails in shallow freshwater marshes. When water levels or vegetation change and snails decline, the kites have little else to eat.
species.habitat: Shallow freshwater marshes and lake edges with open water and emergent plants.
threats: Loss and degradation of freshwater wetlands
Water-level changes that reduce apple snail numbers
Dense invasive vegetation that makes marshes harder to hunt in
identification_tips: Slim hawk with a sharply hooked bill
Males are slate gray with red-orange legs; females and young are brown and streaked
White patch at the base of the tail in flight
how_to_help: Support Everglades restoration that keeps marsh water levels healthy
Watch from a distance and avoid flushing perched birds
Report banded or injured kites to FWC

species.summary: A shy, gray-green crocodilian of coastal mangroves and brackish water.
species.description: The Everglades is the only place in the United States where alligators and crocodiles live side by side. American crocodiles are much shyer than alligators and prefer salty or brackish coastal water.
species.habitat: Mangrove swamps, coastal creeks, and brackish bays in extreme southern Florida.
threats: Loss of coastal nesting habitat to development
Vehicle collisions
Nest predation and changing salinity that affect hatchling survival
identification_tips: Narrow, tapered, V-shaped snout (alligators have a broad U shape)
Gray to olive-gray, lighter than most alligators
Lower teeth stay visible when the mouth is closed
how_to_help: Give crocodiles space and never feed them
Drive slowly near canals and coastal roads
Report injured crocodiles or nuisance concerns to FWC

species.summary: A small ground-nesting songbird found only in the southern Everglades.
species.description: This sparrow lives in marl prairies, where it nests low in the grass. Flooding during nesting season and prairie fires can wipe out a year's chicks.
species.habitat: Marl prairies of the southern Everglades.
threats: Water levels that flood nests during the breeding season
Prairie fires during nesting
Hurricanes and sea-level rise
identification_tips: Small, streaked, olive-gray sparrow with a yellow spot in front of the eye
Lives on the ground in prairie grass and rarely flies far
Confirming it is difficult and is best left to trained surveyors
how_to_help: Support Everglades water management that protects nesting areas
Stay on marked trails in prairie habitat
Share bird sightings through eBird so scientists can see them

species.summary: Florida's largest bat, with big ears that sweep forward like a bonnet.
species.description: The Florida bonneted bat roosts in tree cavities, rock crevices, and sometimes in buildings and bat houses. It has one of the smallest ranges of any bat in the country, confined to southern Florida.
species.habitat: Forests, wetlands, and suburban areas in southern Florida with old trees or other roosts.
threats: Loss of roost trees and natural habitat to development
Hurricane damage to roost sites
A very small population that is hard to study
identification_tips: Wingspan of about 20 inches
Broad ears joined at the base that project over the forehead
Some of its calls are low enough for people to hear
how_to_help: Keep mature trees and dead snags with cavities when it is safe
Do not disturb roosts; use a licensed wildlife professional for bats in buildings
Avoid removing bats from a building during maternity season (mid-April to mid-August)

species.summary: The longest native snake in the United States, harmless to people.
species.description: The eastern indigo snake is a glossy, non-venomous snake that eats a wide range of prey, including other snakes. It is protected, and killing or harassing one is illegal.
species.habitat: Pine flatwoods, hardwood hammocks, and other uplands; often shelters in burrows.
threats: Habitat loss and fragmentation
Road mortality
Loss of the burrows it shelters in
identification_tips: Uniformly glossy blue-black scales
Chin and throat are often reddish or orange
Can reach around 8 feet long
how_to_help: Never kill, capture, or harass an indigo snake
Protect gopher tortoise burrows and other shelter on your property
Report sightings to FWC so biologists can track the population
